articles.title: Social media algorithms: What if you could turn them off?
articles.summary: Australia has proposed a switch to force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.

It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.

Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.

Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.

It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.

He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.

"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."

The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.

Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."

Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.

Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.

But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction ; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health , and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline .

Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.

While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.

"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.

More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.

"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.

"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."

Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram, US court hears

Social media is 'deliberately' addictive

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m).

"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.

There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.

In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise .

"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.

Right-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.

But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.

The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.

However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban ? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.

The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.

Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.

"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation .

On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.

The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.

The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.

Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global.

"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."

Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.

Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."

Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.

Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice.

"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."

If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line .

articles.title: New dinosaur species identified from fossil tucked away in a museum
articles.summary: “It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex,” Morrison said.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A fossil stored in a London museum for more than a century has been identified as a new species of dinosaur.

Researchers say the new dinosaur, Invictibellatrix amberina , was identified from a skull fragment at the Natural History Museum. The fossil was first found by Reginald Walter Tooley, an amateur paleontologist, at the base of a cliff on the Isle of Wight.

After Tooley died, the museum acquired the fossil in 1924, along with more than 1,000 other specimens he had collected.

“It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years,” said the study’s lead author, Dr. Cassius Morrison, in a press release .

Researchers used CT scans to make 3D images of the skull and the area where the dinosaur’s brain would have been. When they compared these images to other meat-eating dinosaurs, they found some unusual features. These included an oval-shaped opening where the spinal cord met the brain and a ridge shaped like an hourglass. These differences led them to decide it was a new species.

Invictibellatrix was part of a group of meat-eating dinosaurs called megaraptorans, which were related to tyrannosaurs . It had a long, narrow head, small arms, and probably had feathers. Its claws were between 4 and 8 inches long. The dinosaur was about 10 to 13 feet long and stood around 5 feet tall, making it one of the smallest and earliest megaraptorans found so far.

Scientists believe it lived in what is now the United Kingdom about 120 million years ago. Its name means ‘unconquered female warrior,’ a reference to the group’s later role as top predators.

“It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex, ” Morrison said.

“ We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight,” he continued. “They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small.”

The researchers published their findings in the journal Royal Society Open Science .

articles.title: How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections
articles.summary: Through statements in English, Iranian officials are emphasising gas prices and issues with the US economy.
articles.body:
In messages that appear to be directed at the American public, Iran has been highlighting the cost of the war that the United States and Israel launched against the country ahead of the United States midterm elections.

Iranian officials have published articles in state-affiliated outlets stressing the disastrous impact of the war on oil prices and the US economy, while Iran’s chief negotiator and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has actively targeted US officials about rising costs and military spending.

Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said Tehran is looking to increase the political cost of the war for Trump by trying to talk directly to the American public.

“It’s not necessarily that they’re trying to get Democrats in power or manipulate US politics in a certain direction, other than just overall increasing the costs on this issue of the Iran war, and just playing that game of information warfare and getting out their own narrative and propaganda as well,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.

Trump’s Republican Party is looking to retain control of the Senate and House of Representatives in next month’s midterm vote. But the Democratic Party, which largely opposes the war with Iran, is mounting a strong challenge across the congressional electoral map, including in areas that have been conservative strongholds for decades, such as Texas .

On Wednesday, Ghalibaf shared a news story on inflation rising to 3.7 percent last month along with a collage of negative headlines on the US economy.

The social media post also featured a comic strip from the Road Runner cartoon showing Wile E Coyote building a catapult that misfires and launches a boulder at him.

“Let’s ‘play the percentages’. Not in odds, but in the % increases,” Ghalibaf wrote in a message to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has been leading the sanctions campaign against Iran.

Bessent said last month that he represents “the house”, likening the economy to a casino while addressing the national debt and bond market.

Ghalibaf’s remark referred to the increase in inflation, underscoring that the cost of living keeps rising due to the war despite Bessent’s assertions.

Days earlier, he shared an image of a ghost shaped like a bell curve, with diesel prices rising and housing affordability and consumer confidence falling.

Since the start of the war on February 28, Iran has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, sending energy prices soaring. In the US, the price of diesel is at an all-time record of $6.33 per gallon (3.8 litres), according to the American Automobile Association, and gas is $4.33, up from less than $3 before the war.

Iran has intensified its attacks on vessels around the strait in recent days after Trump and his aides repeatedly stressed that the waterway is under US control.

The uptick in energy prices has fuelled overall inflation in the economy, leading the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates last month at a time when Trump has been calling for them to be cut to stimulate economic activity.

In a letter to the American public on September 29, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) accused Trump of lying about the cost of the war and the state of the US economy, dismissing the president’s claims that oil prices would soon nosedive.

“Countries around the world have lost their faith in the US economy. Demand for American bonds has plummeted. In fact, countries are starting to offload their US bonds. Soon, the dam will break, and the economy will implode, causing, unfortunately, great pain for Americans for many many years,” the IRGC said.

“Americans need to wake up. They need to wrest control back from corrupt politicians. Now is the time, as the American political system is at its weakest.”

The US midterm elections are seen as a turning point in the conflict – not because of their potential outcome, but because of what Trump might do after the vote.

Trump has suggested that he would either strike a deal with Iran or return to a full-scale war after the November 3 legislative elections. He has also dismissed the idea that the vote will have any impact on his Iran policy.

“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realise is that I’m not running,” Trump said at the United Nations General Assembly last month.

“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election. When it comes to Iran, it doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”

If the Democrats gain control of Congress, they can push for measures to curb Trump’s ability to continue the war, including through withholding funding for the military campaign.

But Toossi said there is a debate within Iran on the potential impact of a Democratic victory in November.

While some point to foreign policy hawks among the Democrats to argue that little would change, others say a midterm defeat would make him politically vulnerable and likely constrain his war powers .

“I don’t think they’re hedging their bets either way, and I don’t think it necessarily affects their overall strategy of increasing the costs [of war] regardless of whatever happens in November,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Washington Post says photographer attacked by Israeli settlers
articles.summary: The Washington Post’s executive editor said Friday that Israeli settlers attacked one of its photojournalists, who was working on assignment in the West Bank. “She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist,” Matt Murray wrote in a statement shared to social platform X. “We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a…
articles.body:
The Washington Post’s executive editor said Friday that Israeli settlers attacked one of its photojournalists, who was working on assignment in the West Bank.

“She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist,” Matt Murray wrote in a statement shared to social platform X . “We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job.”

A video capturing the incident — shared by the Post — appeared to show masked Israeli settlers attacking photographer Heidi Levine while she was on the ground, kicking her in the stomach. Separate posts by independent journalist Andrey Khrzhanovskiy, a pro-Palestinian activist, alleged the assailants also beat her with sticks.

“They took everything. They took all my stuff,” Levine said in the video when Khrzhanovskiy and other nearby journalists came to her aid. “They just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times.”

After a few moments, the masked settlers began chasing Levine and the group that helped her.

Levine’s alleged assault was a part of masked settlers’ attack on a West Bank village’s annual harvest, where the attackers reportedly burned olive trees and threw rocks at Palestinians, according to Reuters , citing witnesses to the incident. The bystanders told the publication that 80 masked people carrying gas canisters had descended upon the gathering.

Palestinian medics treated Levine at a hospital in Ramallah , a city north of Jerusalem, Murray said. He added that she is now “safe.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the attack in a Friday morning statement , saying, “Israel unequivocally condemns violence against anyone—Jews, Arabs, Christians or journalists. Those responsible will be held accountable.”

But Netanyahu also called into question who started the encounter, as “reports indicate some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths,” he said.

The Israeli prime minister added that “masked individuals on both sides [were] hurling objects” and other recordings appear “to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual.”

“The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence,” he concluded.

The Israeli military and Israel Border Police similarly decried the incident and confirmed its forces had responded to it, saying, “All details of the incident will be examined. Upon arriving to the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means.”

“At another location where the confrontation took place, IDF [Israeli Defense Forces] soldiers initially fired warning shots into the air and then fired toward a suspect who ran toward them, carrying a sharp object and posed a threat to them. The confrontation was dispersed,” the Israeli military stated.

articles.title: UK PM adviser’s wife expresses ‘support’ for Palestine Action
articles.summary: Police reviewing social media post by writer Sarah Helm, wife of Burnham’s National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell.
articles.body:
British police are reviewing a social media post by the wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell in which she appears to endorse Palestine Action, a group proscribed in the country as a “terrorist” organisation.

“God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action,” Sarah Helm, a writer who is married to Powell – Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s national security adviser – wrote on X on Thursday.

She was responding to a post defending Irish novelist Sally Rooney , who this week announced her books would no longer be sold in the United Kingdom over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.

A Metropolitan Police spokesperson on Friday said Helm’s post is “being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required”.

A government spokesperson cited by the Reuters news agency said the views expressed in Helm’s post “are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity”.

UK-based activist group Defend Our Juries defended Helm for defying what it called an “absurdly authoritarian ban on Palestine Action”.

“We know of 36 people who have been arrested and had their homes raided for similarly expressing support for Palestine Action on social media,” said a spokesperson for the group.

“We hope Sarah will not face the same treatment for standing up for free speech and Palestinian lives.”

The UK government outlawed Palestine Action in July 2025, after activists from the group broke into a Royal Air Force base and sprayed red paint on two aircraft to protest against UK military support for Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Being a member or a supporter is punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

Since the ban went into effect, police have arrested more than 3,500 people in the UK for alleged support of the group, many of them for holding up placards, according to rights group Amnesty International.

Palestine Action has contested its proscription, but the Court of Appeal upheld it in June .

The UK’s new Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband last month said the government was “looking at” the Palestine Action ban, adding that he did not believe mass arrests resulting from its proscription were “anyone’s intent”.

articles.body: Depending on where you live, winter often brings snow. Those falling flakes can be beautiful (and even fun), but they also call for some preparation. A good ice scraper makes quick work of a frosted windshield, and hand warmers help you stay cozy on frigid mornings. Just as essential is a reliable pair of snow boots. The right boots keep your feet warm and dry, and if they’re supportive, they can also help you stay steady on slick, icy ground. According to experts, arch support is one of the most important features to look for. “As a podiatrist, I cannot stress enough the importance of choosing the right snow boots for maintaining good foot health and comfort, especially when it comes to arch support,” says Dr. Miguel Cunha, a podiatrist and founder of Gotham Footcare in New York City. To help you find a pair that keeps your feet warm and well-supported all season, I asked Cunha and other podiatrists what to look for when shopping, as well as which boots they recommend. The best snow boots with arch support Below are snow boots recommended by Cunha, along with some highly- rated options I included using the guidance he provided. Best snow boots for women “Though a pricier option, I recommend the Joan of Arctic Women’s Waterproof Boots for their exceptional arch support, durable design, and superior insulation,” says Cunha. The boot has a handcrafted vulcanized rubber outsole with herringbone tread for grip in icy conditions and a waterproof suede upper for style and comfort. These boots also have a washable felt inner for additional warmth. The footbed has a built-in arch and is lightly cushioned for comfort. Seam-sealed construction and insulation keep your feet warm and dry in temperatures up to -40 degrees Fahrenheit, according to Kamik. Cunha also likes that they have a moisture-wicking lining to ensure your feet stay comfortable and a bungee lacing system for easy wear. A molded, removable insole provides support, and the rubber outsole has deep treads to keep you steady on slippery patches. Plus, a faux fur collar adds style. The rubber bottoms on these boots keep moisture out, deep lugs in the sole add traction and a fleece lining gives them warmth, according to the brand. “I recommend The North Face Shellista Mid Boots as a supportive boot for winter conditions,” says Cunha, who notes that the boot offers good arch support and adjustable laces for a custom fit. These boots have a waterproof leather upper, rubber bottom and extra quilted stitching around the ankle for added support. They also have insoles with built-in arch support and medium cushioning. These boots have a neoprene upper that provides flexibility for movement and a rubber bottom to keep feet dry. There is a fleece lining for warmth and comfort and the boot is rated to keep feet comfortable even in -40-degree Fahrenheit temperatures, according to the brand. The insole is contoured for support and padded to keep your foot cushioned. Best snow boots for men These boots are made with Columbia’s proprietary technology, which makes these boots breathable while still keeping out cold and wetness, according to the brand. They have a waterproof leather upper and rubber sole with deep treads that provide traction wherever you’re walking. The lightweight midsole has a supportive arch and lots of cushioning for comfort. “Snow boots that have somewhat of a slight heel less than three-quarters of an inch in relation to the front are actually better for you than shoes that are completely flat because it takes the stress off the Achilles which can help with the alignment of your posture, ankles, knees and spine,” says Cunha. These boots have a slightly elevated heel, along with a waterproof suede upper and rubber shell to keep snow out and keep feet warm even when it gets down to -25 degrees Fahrenheit outside. Offering protection in weather as low as -40 degrees Fahrenheit, these boots have a removable liner and a cushioned, contoured footbed. According to the brand, they also have a rustproof speed lacing system, making it easy to get in and out of them. This Chelsea-style boot is built for everyday winter wear. A waterproof leather upper and breathable membrane keep feet dry, thick insulation adds warmth, and a heat-shield footbed and stability shank offer support. The 5-inch shaft is shorter than many snow boots, so it’s best suited to city sidewalks or areas without deep snow. Why you need snow boots with arch support “Proper arch support is critical for maintaining foot alignment and reducing strain, especially when wearing snow boots for prolonged periods of time,” says Cunha. He notes that snow boots are usually worn in cold, wet conditions on uneven terrain like snow and ice. “Without adequate support, the foot can flatten or overpronate, which may lead to discomfort, pain, or long-term foot issues like plantar fasciitis.” Supportive boots can also keep you safer by making you steadier on your feet. “Choosing the right snow boots with good arch support helps distribute weight evenly across your feet, which improves stability,” says Cunha. That added stability is especially valuable on slick or uneven ground, where a misstep can easily lead to a fall. How I picked the best snow boots with arch support If you are looking for snow boots with arch support, the podiatrists I spoke with said these are the top things to pay attention to while shopping: Built-in arches: “Look for built-in arch support with anatomical contoured footbed to support the natural shape of your foot,” says Cunha. “This will help with foot alignment and reduce strain, especially during extended wear.” Support: A sole on the firmer side will provide more support than a flimsy one. “This will provide more shock absorption, and in turn will result in less foot pain such as arch pain and heel pain,” says Cunha. “Snow boots should also offer strong ankle support to help stabilize your feet and legs, to help prevent injuries on uneven terrain, snow, and ice.” Wide toe box: Look for snow boots with a wide toe box. This gives the forefoot more wiggle room and will place less aggravation on feet that suffer from bunions and hammertoes, says Cunha.Quality materials: At the end of the day, your snow boots need to keep your feet warm and dry and also provide traction to help you walk through ice and snow. “Snow boots made from rubber, latex, and PVC (Polyvinyl Chloride- Synthetic plastic) are effective at keeping water out of a boot because these materials are impermeable to molecules of water,” says Cunha, who particularly likes rubber because it’s the most durable. “Snow boots made with thicker rubber will last longer and retain their shape over time,” he says. articles.title: Police feared Andrew might delay access by saying his home was King's
articles.summary: Legal records have emerged which show why police wanted to search the royal's home and what they were looking for.
articles.body:
Thames Valley Police feared Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor might have tried to stop officers entering his home in Sandringham by saying it belonged to the King, according to legal documents.

Senior officers were concerned the King's brother could argue it was not his property, and that separate legal permission would have to be sought before officers could enter it.

Delaying access would have risked the loss of evidence, the force said.

The background to Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest in February has emerged in legal documents, when police asked a judge for warrants to raid the former prince's homes.

Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest came after the US Department of Justice published material which showed his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The BBC has approached Mountbatten-Windsor's representatives for comment and he has denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

The arrest of the former prince, on 19 February, was on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

Warrants used to search Andrew's homes were unlawful, court says

Why was Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor arrested and what happens next?

How Andrew's 11-hour detention on his birthday played out

On 18 February, Thames Valley Police asked for permission from the Central Criminal Court for warrants to search Wood Farm in Sandringham and Royal Lodge in Windsor.

The request included the police outlining the scenarios in which they believed they would need search warrants to ensure access to the properties.

They feared that Mountbatten-Windsor or his legal team would want to see "judicial authority" before allowing the police to enter, the documents show.

The police were concerned that Mountbatten-Windsor or his representatives could argue that the Sandringham Estate was the property of King Charles - and that it would be a slow process getting a separate right of access.

Such a delay would "frustrate the nature and purpose of the search," said the police, in their application for search warrants.

There was also a concern that no one would be present at the property and that media attention could be drawn to the police presence outside while not being able to enter.

Any of those delays could have meant the police would have been unable to gather the evidence they wanted, they argued - and "given the gravity of this investigation", the police asked for search warrants.

In separate documents filed as part of Mountbatten-Windsor's legal challenge against the warrants, he said: "These assertions were no more than speculation."

The documents also detail the type of information the police were seeking inside the properties.

They say: "Paper-work, diaries, business records or other documentary evidence of AMW's [Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's] time as Special Representative for Trade and Investment.

"Further evidence as to any action, communication, comment or in relation to matters following the release of material by the FBI concerning the late Jeffrey Epstein as AMW will be aware that Thames Valley Police is conducting an assessment.

"Specifically mobile phone(s) and computer(s) [to include electronic notebooks, surfaces, iPads and any older electronic devices," which could have held information about links to Epstein at the time when Mountbatten-Windsor had been the UK's trade envoy."

The documents show the search of Royal Lodge, Mountbatten-Windsor's former home in Windsor, continued until 24 February.

They also reveal his police interview at Aylesham Police Station began at 15:00 GMT and he was released under investigation at 18:36.

The legal documents give details of why the police wanted to talk to Mountbatten-Windsor, including the claim that when he was a UK trade envoy he had forwarded Jeffrey Epstein official reports from official visits to Singapore, Vietnam, China and Hong Kong.

There was also a claim, arising from emails in the Epstein files released in the US, that Mountbatten-Windsor had briefed Epstein on investment opportunities in Afghanistan.

Also mentioned is the suggestion Mountbatten-Windsor held meetings with a private investment firm and then suggesting to Epstein that he might invest in the company.

The legal documents have emerged after a High Court hearing earlier this month in which Thames Valley Police accepted the warrants it used to search Mountbatten-Windsor's homes were unlawful.

Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers used a judicial review to successfully challenge the actions of the force's chief constable and the Central Criminal Court in the build-up to his arrest.

Thames Valley Police's position was that they had applied for search warrants under section eight and nine of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 at a hearing at the Central Criminal Court the day before the search.

That court determined that only section eight search warrants were needed and they were granted on that basis - but subsequently, a legal challenge has established that the court should have issued them under the section nine.

But items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence.

Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.

Thames Valley Police force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.

At the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.

However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."

articles.title: 'Well-known' man asks court to stop publication of sexual offence allegation
articles.summary: The unnamed individual asks London's High Court to prevent the publication of "serious allegations".
articles.body:
An individual described as "well-known" has asked London's High Court to prevent two media organisations from publishing "serious allegations", including of a sexual nature, against him.

The court heard he had submitted medical evidence saying that if the allegations were made public this would "almost certainly" lead to him "attempting to take his own life", and that the prospect of publication had already led to two suicide attempts.

The court was told that Independent Television News and Guardian News & Media had carried out an investigation into the individual's "conduct over a period of years".

The individual, who has been granted anonymity in the court proceedings, denies the allegations.

The court was told that following an investigation that ITN, which produces news for ITV and Channel 4, and Guardian News & Media, which publishes the Guardian, sent two letters to the the well-known individual in the spring of 2026.

As well as denying the allegations, the individual responded with medical reports stating that there was a risk to his life if the information was published.

At an injunction hearing at London's High Court, lawyers representing ITN and Guardian News & Media said that "it would be wrong" for the court to "restrain publication" when the "law provides for a detailed and well-established scheme by which the interests of those at risk of suicide is specially protected by NHS mental health professionals".

The court has also granted anonymity to other individuals in the case.

Two individuals who have agreed to be identified in any ITN and Guardian News & Media report concerning the allegations were given anonymity in the current proceedings by High Court judge Mr Justice Nicklin. The nature of the allegations or how these two journalistic sources relate to them is not known.

A third journalistic source for the ITN and Guardian News & Media investigation has also been granted anonymity in the current proceedings. She has alleged that she was the victim of a sexual offence by the well-known individual.

The court will decide whether the ITN and Guardian News & Media will be permanently prevented from naming the well-known individual and publishing the allegations against him at a trial due to be held later this month.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line .

articles.title: Kenya records third Ebola case, linked to first patient who died
articles.summary: Nairobi says 65-year-old female patient in quarantine with Bundibugyo strain; no signs of community transmission.
articles.body:
Kenya has recorded its third case of the Bundibugyo virus disease – a strain of Ebola that has killed thousands of people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) – 10 days after reporting its first case and death in Nairobi.

The latest confirmed case – a 65-year-old woman – was a “primary contact and a close relative of the first and second cases”, Kenya’s Health Ministry said in a statement on Friday, adding that the patient has been in quarantine since October 6.

After developing symptoms, she was isolated and then tested positive for the virus, it added in a statement.

“Once she developed fever, sore throat and malaise, she was isolated and specimen collected for testing. She tested positive for Ebola,” the Health Ministry said. “She was diagnosed early and is currently receiving ⁠⁠supportive care improving her ⁠⁠chances of recovery.”

Kenya’s cases are linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, which is the second-largest on record globally ⁠ ⁠with more than 9,000 cases and over 4,300 deaths since it was officially detected in May.

Kenya’s ⁠⁠first case emerged last ⁠⁠week after a Kenyan man, who had been ill in the DRC about a month before travelling by road ‌‌to Uganda, flew to Nairobi on October 3, where a relative drove him to ‌‌the ‌‌hospital. He died on October 5.

In its statement on X, the Health Ministry moved to reassure the public that there was no community spread of the disease and that the risk to the Kenyan public remained low.

Out of 130 contacts listed, 127 had been traced and were in quarantine, it said.

Efforts to control the spread of the Ebola outbreak have been complicated because the Bundibugyo strain has no licensed vaccine. Research is under way to develop one or more vaccines that work against the strain and some of these vaccines are already in the early phases of testing in humans.

Transparency demands over Ebola response funds

The new case in Kenya was reported as Africa’s ‌‌top public health body and Congolese health authorities called ⁠⁠for greater transparency in how Ebola response funds are used.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said financial information provided by aid organisations indicated that ⁠⁠more than $700m of donor money was unaccounted for.

Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of ‌‌the Africa CDC, told the Reuters news agency that international donors disbursed about $962m to organisations ⁠⁠implementing Ebola response activities in DRC, rather ⁠⁠than to the government.

Kaseya said those organisations reported receiving $228m, of which $127m had ⁠⁠been spent and roughly $100m remained available.

But he said it was too early to speak of embezzlement.

In a post on X, Congolese Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba warned aid groups were required to provide details on funding ‌‌sources to his ministry or risk being barred from working ‌‌in ‌‌DRC and blacklisted across Africa.

Meanwhile, on the ground in the DRC, Ebola cases have been detected in a new province bordering the Central African Republic, two health officials told Reuters on Thursday.

The two cases were confirmed in North Ubangi, the eighth Congolese province affected by the Bundibugyo outbreak, the officials said. Congolese authorities have not yet officially announced the outbreak has spread to North Ubangi.

articles.title: Police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser's wife
articles.summary: Downing Street says Sarah Helm, the wife of Jonathan Powell, "does not represent the government in any capacity".
articles.body:
Police are assessing a social media post by the wife of the government's national security adviser Jonathan Powell which referenced Palestine Action, a group labelled a terrorist organisation by the Home Office.

Sarah Helm wrote on the social media site X: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."

She was responding to a discussion on Sky News about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.

A No 10 spokeswoman said Helm was "an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity". The BBC has attempted to contact Helm for comment.

On Friday, a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: "We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action.

"It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required."

Reform UK MP Danny Kruger has written to the prime minister raising concerns about Helm's post.

The Campaign Against Antisemitism said the post was "gobsmacking".

"Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country's national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post," the group said.

However, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Sarah Helm is speaking absolute common sense and should be commended for her bravery."

He called for Palestine Action to be de-proscribed "immediately", calling its official labelling as a terror group "ludicrous and authoritarian".

Helm is an author and journalist, who has previously worked at the Sunday Times and as a foreign correspondent for the Independent.

Palestine Action describes itself as a "direct action movement" that uses "disruptive tactics".

Earlier this year, four of the group's activists were jailed after causing £1.2m of damage at a UK site of an Israel-based defence firm.

In 2025, the UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist group, saying it would not "tolerate" organisations that put the UK's national security at risk.

The proscription made it a criminal offence to belong to or support Palestine Action, punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

The government's decision triggered a wave of protests, which saw an estimated 3,700 people arrested in the UK for publicly expressing their support for the group.

Around 2,500 have been charged, but the cases have not gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription is due to be heard in the Supreme Court next month.

Powell began his government career as a diplomat but later served as an adviser in Tony Blair's government, where he was credited with negotiating a peace deal in Northern Ireland.

In 2024, Sir Keir Starmer appointed him as national security adviser, a position he retained when Andy Burnham became prime minister.

articles.title: Bryan Kohberger fights to remove judge who called him 'worst of the worst,' questioned his honesty
articles.summary: Bryan Kohberger's new attorney accuses Latah County prosecutors of dodging key arguments in his motion to disqualify Judge Steven Hippler from the case.
articles.body: Bryan Kohberger's new lawyer is taking another swing at Idaho prosecutors in his fight to have the judge who called his client a "faceless coward" removed from post-conviction proceedings. Court-appointed attorney Greg Rauch is accusing Latah County prosecutors of "regurgitating" rules rather than addressing concerns raised in his motion to disqualify Judge Steven Hippler from the case. Hippler said Kohberger, 31, "slithered" into the victims' home before committing a crime that made him "the worst of the worst" after the killer admitted guilt last year. At issue, according to Rauch, "is how [Hippler's] statements about counsel’s preparation and [Kohberger's] capacity for truthfulness bear on the disputes it may now decide, in combination with the myriad of other statements made." KOHBERGER PROSECUTORS SAY NO AS IDAHO KILLER TRIES TO BOOT JUDGE WHO CALLED HIM A 'FACELESS COWARD' And when addressing the fact that there would be no allocution or explanation from Kohberger, the judge also questioned whether Kohberger even possessed the capacity to say something truthful. "Even if I could force him to speak, which legally I cannot, how could anyone ever be assured that what he speaks is the truth?" Hippler asked during sentencing. "Do we really believe, after all of this, he is capable of speaking the truth, or of giving up something of himself to help the very people whose lives he destroyed? Rather, I suspect the so-called reason would be dished out in enticing self-serving and aggrandizing untruthful bits, leaving people wanting more information, more insight, and thus enhancing even further the power he seeks to hold." BRYAN KOHBERGER DIDN'T UNDERSTAND WHAT HE WAS DOING WHEN HE PLEADED GUILTY: UNSEALED MEMO Rauch wrote that "of course" judges can deny defense motions, "condemn terrible crimes," and go on to preside over post-conviction claims. BRYAN KOHBERGER'S NEW LAWYER SAYS KEY QUESTIONS MAY SOON GET ANSWERS IN COURT "The question is not whether someone might criticize the Court, but whether an informed, reasonable observer could question its impartiality in light of this connected record," he wrote. And it's not just that Hippler tore into Kohberger at sentencing. He has also taken issue with a June scheduling order days before Kohberger surprised the country and pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty. "This motion does not rest upon one adverse ruling, one harsh statement, or the mere fact that the judge who presided over Bryan Kohberger’s criminal case has been assigned to his post-conviction proceeding," Rauch wrote in his initial 22-page motion on Aug. 27. "It rests upon the extraordinary convergence of all of them." Hippler had rejected a request for more time for Kohberger's previous defense lawyer, Anne Taylor, and in a June 26 order, described her complaints about discovery as "ultimately empty" while suggesting she was simply trying to delay his trial. IDAHO PROSECUTORS ACCUSE BRYAN KOHBERGER OF 'FISHING' TO FIND BETTER ARGUMENTS FOR BID TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA Six days later, at a change-of-plea hearing, Hippler asked Taylor, "Have you been able to do all the discovery you feel necessary?" "Yes, Your Honor," she replied. BRYAN KOHBERGER WAIVED HIS APPEAL RIGHTS BUT PLANS ON PURSUING POST-CONVICTION RELIEF Prosecutors, in an opposition to the motion filed earlier this month, wrote that Kohberger had failed to show Hippler "is biased." FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Outgoing Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Bill Thompson, who announced his retirement earlier this week, and Deputy Prosecuting Attorney Keith Scholl wrote that Hippler's statements about Kohberger after he'd admitted to killing four innocent students were not unusual or out of line. BRYAN KOHBERGER’S 2027 HEARING IS NOT GUARANTEED AS IDAHO SEEKS QUICK DISMISSAL "In our case, the sentencing remarks are not enough to show bias, and the required showing of perceived bias cannot be tied to this Court's capacity to fairly adjudicate any [post-conviction relief] claims alleged in this case but rather puts this Court in the best position to adjudicate them as the legislature and the Idaho Supreme Court's rules intend," they wrote. BRYAN KOHBERGER'S POST-CONVICTION RELIEF BID ENABLED BY FLAWED PLEA DEAL, PSYCHOLOGIST ARGUES Rauch also argued that Hippler could voluntarily recuse himself from the case to avoid any appearance of partiality. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS In the new 12-page filing, Rauch also argued that prosecutors have attributed concessions to his client that were never made, mischaracterized his initial motion and failed to address some of the arguments he did make in it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB "The State’s Response does not resolve this motion by repeating the ordinary rule, supplying concessions Petitioner never made, or calling the disputed statements routine," Rauch wrote. Kohberger is attempting to undo his guilty plea in the University of Idaho student murders that killed Madison Mogen, 21, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20, in November 2022. "Reassignment would change the judge, not the evidence or the governing law." articles.title: Oregon school shooting victims include 5-year-old whose family is ‘broken and lost’
articles.summary: The three children and a teacher killed in a special education classroom at an Oregon elementary school Thursday included a 5-year-old boy whose family said they are “broken and lost” after the shooting.
articles.body: The three children and a teacher killed in a special education classroom at an Oregon elementary school Thursday included a 5-year-old boy whose family said they are “broken and lost” after the shooting. Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old with long curly hair, was identified as one of the victims by a family member. The shooting occurred at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday. Officials said an armed bystander fatally shot the teen gunman, putting an end to the shooting spree. Rhoam’s mother, Kelik Summer posted to a Facebook group last night, saying Thursday was “the worst day of my life. My son Rhoam was killed in a school shooting.” “We are broken and lost, but are surrounded by friends and family who are keeping us safe,” Summer wrote. Several parents told NBC News the shooting happened in a special education classroom. Police have not confirmed that detail. A 7-year-old who was in a wheelchair and another teacher were also critically injured in the shooting. “There are simply no words for the loss that we have suffered today,” Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler said at a community vigil hours after the tragedy. The injured teacher was identified by her husband as Rebecca Drury. “We are incredibly grateful for the outpouring of support, prayers, and well-wishes following yesterday’s tragedy at Silver Rail Elementary,” he wrote in a statement. “The kindness and concern shown to our family and everyone affected mean more than we can express.” “Right now, our focus is on my wife, Becky, and her recovery, and on supporting our family through an unimaginably difficult time,” he wrote. “We respectfully ask for privacy and space as we navigate the days ahead.” The person who took down the gunman was identified as Kaylub Giamanco, 36, a father of two whose students attend the elementary school, his brother, Kyle Giamanco, told NBC News. Kaylub Giamanco is a hero, his brother said. Part of the reason his brother does not want to speak out is because he doesn’t feel like a hero — he can’t get the children out of his head and feels guilty he didn’t save more people, Kyle Giamanco said. Kyle Giamanco also said he is friends with the family of the 7-year-old child who is in the hospital. The child, who is in a wheelchair and was shot in the face, is recovering from surgery.

articles.summary: Joe Rogan defended Shane Gillis after his SNL monologue about gym attire sparked backlash, arguing the comedian's joke isn't rooted in misogyny.
articles.body: Podcaster Joe Rogan defended comedian Shane Gillis after his Saturday Night Live monologue after a joke about women who film themselves while working out in revealing clothing went viral. Gillis, known for politically incorrect humor, drew backlash from the left for his monologue while hosting SNL last week, joking about "going to the public gym as a fat guy." "Also, I haven’t been to the gym in so long. I didn’t know women just dressed like whores now? Look, I’m sorry. There’s no other way to describe ... Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts. Have you seen the shorts?" he asked. "And don’t look! You’re not allowed to look. For real. Don’t look because they are filming. I’m in the background in like 10 TikToks right now." SHANE GILLIS SHRUGS OFF, MOCKS CHELSEA HANDLER'S OUTRAGE OVER HIS JOKES AT KEVIN HART ROAST The comments drew uproar and accusations of misogyny from the left. Rogan brought up the backlash as he spoke to influencer Cody Tucker on his podcast Thursday. "I guess the word ‘whore’ is what gets them. I get it. I get that you get upset. Well, it's also because like real misogyny actually exists," Rogan said. "So, when you see a guy joking around about a woman dressing like a whore, you connect it to horrible thoughts, like horrible actions, like real actual evil men that actually. Because, like, there's a lot of men that genuinely hate women. Shane Gillis is not one of them," Rogan said. "And he's a great guy. It's just a joke." articles.title: Trump hosted a dinner with – wait for it – Stephen A Smith, Kid Rock and Bill Maher
articles.summary: Trump hosted Kid Rock, Bill Maher, and Stephen A. Smith for a dinner that Kid Rock called "epic" during his "Fox & Friends" appearance Friday.
articles.body: President Donald Trump hosted a dinner on Thursday night with, wait for it, singer Kid Rock, HBO host Bill Maher and ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith. Kid Rock, whose real name is Robert Ritchie, mentioned the dinner during a Friday morning appearance on Fox News’ "Fox & Friends," calling the gathering "epic." The singer said the four men agreed on at least one point: "Socialism and communism have no place to have a foothold in our government." It's not entirely clear why Trump assembled that particular group for dinner. However, Rock said he and Maher recently joined Trump for a separate meal that also included UFC president Dana White. Apparently, Smith served as the sports representative this time. BILL MAHER REVEALS HE'S HAVING DINNER WITH TRUMP AGAIN, SAYS HE WAS 'REALLY NICE' BY TEXT To the group's credit, there was at least some political diversity at the table. Kid Rock is an avid Trump supporter. Maher is a liberal who has become increasingly critical of both parties and the progressive left. Smith is, well, politically inconsistent. We suspect Smith played the role of proud moderate Thursday night, as he often does when appearing on conservative radio and television. That version of Smith can sound quite different from the one who appears on SiriusXM and his YouTube channel, where he is far more sensitive to the concerns of liberals and what he frequently calls the Black community. Smith says he will address the dinner Friday night on his podcast. Our prediction: He will downplay the chummy nature of the gathering, stress that attending dinner with Trump does not mean he supports him, and claim he pushed the president on racial issues. He will then offer a somewhat different account the next time a conservative interviews him. Maher, meanwhile, is probably the most likely member of the group to provide a straightforward account of what actually happened. We do not doubt the evening was as entertaining as Kid Rock suggests. Still, the dinner is notable for another reason. Trump remains one of the few major politicians in 2026 who regularly sits down with people who openly disagree with him. Few political commentators have been more consistently critical of Trump than Maher, including after the two first had dinner together last year. In any event, a dinner with Trump, Kid Rock, Maher, and Smith could be good fodder for Saturday Night Live this weekend. articles.title: Brittany Mahomes stuns fans with her gym picture, Fitzy obliterates Bo Nix & is college football going to die?
articles.summary: Thursday Night Football saw Bo Nix rank dead last among 701 quarterbacks in average pass length as Ryan Fitzpatrick delivered a brutal takedown.
articles.body: Happy Friday — have we all cleansed ourselves of that Thursday Night Football game last night? Goodness gracious. I thought I was immune to bad quarterback play given I've been a Dolphins fan for 25 years, but even I was disgusted by what I saw. Sure, l may be a little biased because I had RJ Harvey at OVER 3.5 receptions and Bo Nix couldn't get him the ball in the second half if his life depended on it, but still ... It was bad. It was gross. Wait till you see what Ryan Fitzpatrick had to say about it. Lordy. Before that, though ... welcome to a Friday Nightcaps — the one where Brittany Mahomes hits the gym and shows America she still very much has the fastball. What else? I've got college football continuing down its dangerous path with a 24-team playoff, the aforementioned Fitzpatrick takedown, and I don't do much soccer, but you HAVE to see this penalty kick from earlier in the week. I have no idea who this cat is, where this game was played, or who these teams are ... but I'm all in. I can't stop watching. It's mesmerizing. You'll see. OK, grab you a Sears Christmas catalog and start circling things to celebrate National Department Store Day, and settle in for a Friday 'Cap! Brittany Mahomes puts an exclamation point on this week's 'gym attire' debate Man, do I miss department stores. They were the best. Sure, some still kinda-sorta exist — I still have a Dillard's in my town, somehow — but it's not the same. And today's youth will never, ever know the feeling. What a pleasure. Sears, Macy's, JCPenney, Dillard's — all absolute staples in a shopping mall back in the '80s and '90s. They'd be in the four separate corners of the mall, and it was just a choose-your-own-adventure book every time you pulled into the parking lot. Which entrance do we wanna choose? Do we feel like going through the Macy's perfume section to get to the Auntie Anne's in the food court because it's a quicker route? Is it gonna be weird when we have to walk by the Victoria's Secret with our parents? What are the chances we can convince them to give us some quarters for the arcade? Wait, are those teriyaki chicken bites on a toothpick in the food court free?! Man, we had it all. It was perfect. And for those who want just a little taste, here's a throwback to what I still consider the greatest commercial of all time, even all these years later: Core memory unlocked. Chills, every time. That thing used to play 27 times an hour back in the day. It didn't matter the channel, you knew you were getting the Sears AC commercial at some point during Gilligan's Island. What a time to be alive. What a country. OK, let's jump back to 2026 (sadly) and get this class started with Brittany Mahomes hitting the gym and reminding America she's still very much in her prime: Bo Nix was horrible last night "Archives never expire," Mahomes captioned the above post. No idea what that means, but who am I to question it? I haven't been to a gym in a decade. Welcome back to class, Brittany! Been a while. Some folks tend to forget about Brittany Mahomes in Kansas City with Taylor Swift now a permanent resident, but I'd tread lightly with that one. She's still very much the First Lady of Arrowhead. Don't get it twisted. The Chiefs still haven't lost a game this season, and I don't expect that to change this weekend against the Chargers. Patrick's locked in, and so is Brittany Mahomes. Good luck, NFL. Now, speaking of the AFC West ... Let's go ahead and check in with Ryan Fitzpatrick after Denver's huge OT win last night. Surely morale is HIGH right now ... Right? Bo, penalty kicks & college football's big move "Bo Nix is not playing competitively. It’s almost disrespectful to the quarterback position how he’s playing football right now." My goodness. What an absolute butt-chewing from Ryan Fitzpatrick here. I've never seen an analyst just obliterate a player like that ... after a win! Some folks are jumping all over Fitzy today, by the way. I think that's ridiculous. He's 100000% right in everything he said. Everything. Bo Nix was atrocious last night. Denver was beyond anemic on offense. Nix finished with 107 yards on 17 completions, and barely — and I mean barely — threw the ball beyond the line of scrimmage. In fact, according to CBS researcher Doug Clawson, he currently ranks 701st out of 701 qualified quarterbacks over the last two decades (!!!) in average pass length (4.9 air yards per attempt). That's indescribably bad. It's unfathomable. I watched Tua Tagovailoa dink and dunk for years in Miami. Bo Nix last night made Tua look like Dan Marino! And everyone's jumping on Fitzpatrick for ... being mean? Give me a break. Grow up. OK, let's rapid-fire this Friday class into a big weekend of FOOTBALL! First up? For those who missed it, college football is closing in on a 24-team playoff starting next season. Twenty-four. I don't know about you, but it makes me sad: So, we're going to lose conference championship games, which is a huge bummer. They obviously still don't mean quite as much as they used to, but that first Saturday in December is always one of the best Saturdays of the year. It's gone now. That's obviously a con. As for the a pro? Well, we do get a ton of actual playoff games on campuses. That's a no-brainer. My biggest issue with the current format is the lack of on-campus games. It's silly. Most of these games should be on campus. It's what makes college football so great. Do I think this will kill college football like a lot of folks are forecasting today? No. Do I think "November games are going to be totally useless" like a lot of folks are forecasting today? No. There will still be important games in November. But ... The regular season as a whole will absolutely lose some juice. Can't really argue that. The college football regular season used to be the best regular season in all of sports because the margin for error was so thin. It's why Tim Tebow famously cried after losing to Ole Miss back in 2008. That's gone now. Losing 2, 3, or even 4 games in some cases won't kill you anymore. That's a bummer. A big one. I'm quite sure you all have opinions on this. Believe me, I see the OutKick newsletter email account. It's loaded today. So ... let me know what you think! Zach.Dean@OutKick.com. (Gulp). CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP OK, that's it for today — and this week! Good work, everyone. On the way out, let's go from football to futbol and end our week with the greatest penalty kick you've ever seen. Have a big October weekend, everyone.

articles.title: Chris Mason: Burnham and Swinney tussle over where power lies in Scotland
articles.summary: UK political debate has a distinctly Scottish feel after SNP's annual conference, says the BBC's political editor Chris Mason.
articles.body:
UK political debate has had a distinctly Scottish feel these last few days.

As the Scottish National Party has gathered for its annual conference at the Event Complex on the outskirts of Aberdeen, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has been in Paisley and Edinburgh and the prime minister has been in Motherwell.

The SNP is buoyant, its activists gathering for the first time since it won, in May, a fifth consecutive Scottish Parliament election, albeit with fewer seats than they won in 2021.

Next year will mark the moment the party has been in devolved power at Holyrood for 20 years.

It is quite the contrast with where the SNP found itself just two years ago, pulverised by the landslide at the general election in 2024 where Labour gained 36 seats from the SNP .

As I wrote a year ago , the SNP's critics point to what they see as a dismal domestic record, on the NHS and the number of deaths among drug addicts, for instance.

The SNP counter Scotland has more police officers per person than England and Wales and the highest spend per school pupil in the UK.

No matter the arguments, the result in May was clear - the SNP leader and First Minister John Swinney has his own mandate. Little wonder, given the state of the party when he took the job, that the conference brochure has a front page photo of a smiling Swinney cradling a glass of whisky.

And remember it wasn't just an electoral pummelling the SNP was dealing with, but the jaw dropping details which culminated in the jailing of Peter Murrell, the party's former chief executive - and estranged husband of the former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon - for embezzling more than £400,000 from the party .

Swinney now looks ahead to a parliamentary term with all that behind them and a new prime minister to deal with in Downing Street.

Burnham and Swinney share a diagnosis that Westminster has failed to deliver and political power is better administered closer to people than it ever has been.

But, crucially, the prime minister sees the "drama" of the constant questions around Scottish independence as a distraction.

For Swinney, independence has been and remains his lifelong political goal.

We have had a glimpse this week as to how that dynamic between the two men may play out.

Burnham's critics, including the SNP, have seen this former Mancunian mayor's devolutionary instincts as having a distinctly English flavour. The prime minister, on his trip to New College Lanarkshire, sought to counter that.

"I do want a good growth in every postcode here, and in the rest of the UK, and I want to work with the first minister to deliver it. We won't agree on everything, but we can agree on something," he said.

"I want us to design a new model together of regional economic empowerment across Scotland, one that puts control in the hands of local people."

Burnham has offered to devolve powers on localised employment support, currently held by the Department of Work and Pensions.

Both he and the Secretary of State for Scotland, Douglas Alexander, said Scotland was "one of the most centralised nations in Europe", an assertion flatly rejected by Swinney.

Scotland's first minister has said he wants "much more opportunity for a regional dimension to take forward skills, economic opportunity and planning" and his team acknowledge this vision includes overlaps with the regional combined authorities seen in parts of England, albeit without mayors .

It will be intriguing to observe, given the rivalry and grit that exists between Labour and the SNP, how things develop beyond the prime minister's speech.

Here in Aberdeen, activists have seized upon the prime minister's reflections on Brexit to argue that if he can revisit the outcome of the referendum in 2016 on the European Union, Scots should be able to revisit the one in 2014 on independence.

There have been plenty of mentions too of an exchange in the Commons last month between SNP MP Chris Law and Andy Burnham, when Burnham suggested another Scottish independence referendum could be held, if public opinion showed demand for one.

SNP folk think - perhaps hope - this represents the prime minister's authentic view.

He and Downing Street have seen sought to squash this idea and he said he wanted to "move on" from a debate about Scottish independence.

Privately, senior SNP figures accept the authority to sanction another referendum lies with Westminster and the UK government says no. So, their focus is seeking to steadily build the case for independence in how they choose to govern.

Within the party, a new group called, you guessed it, "Independence" has been set up.

Speaking at its launch event, the SNP's former Policy Convener Toni Giugliano argued that "countries don't become independent by waiting for permission. They do so when support becomes unstoppable and when a national consensus for change is built".

Furthermore, he argued, fundamental questions about what an independent Scotland would look and feel like must be answered now - such as the currency that would be used and how the state pension would work.

For now, the tussle is more short term, as the SNP ponders when the prime minister might call a general election.

Buoyed by its recent victory at Holyrood, the party senses Labour vulnerability in the swathe of seats Labour took from them two years ago.

articles.title: Five women in Trump’s world who made headlines in last 15 days: Katie Zacharia overtakes Anthony Scaramucci in record of shortest tenure
articles.summary: Anthony Scaramucci served as White House communications director for 11 days, from July 21 to July 31, 2017.
articles.body: Anthony Scaramucci served as White House communications director for 11 days, from July 21 to July 31, 2017. The record of the shortest tenure in the Trump world is likely to be broken by Katie Zacharia, the new press secretary who was panned on the very first day on the job. Then she appeared on Fox News' Sean Hannity show where she was grilled in such a way that political commentators believed that Hannity must have had the go-ahead from the top because Katie Zacharia was 'set to fail'.Katie ZachariaTrump announced on October 9 that Zacharia would replace Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary. She had worked as a spokeswoman for the Department of Homeland Security earlier in 2026 and was a senior communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group. Trump described her as a loyal supporter and a member of the MAGA movement.But the appointment quickly became overshadowed by questions about her professional credentials.Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer and had previously worked at a law firm in Beijing. Her professional profile also listed a general counsel role at Fix California, an advocacy group founded by Trump ally Ric Grenell. Reports suggested that there was no record showing she was registered as an attorney or a member of the bar in any US state or the District of Columbia.Trump was asked about Zacharia's law practice to which the president did not have any answer, and he turned to Zacharia togive the answer. Zacharia said she practised when she was in China. Turns out, she never passed a bar exam and was never a licensed attorney.By October 16, Trump was publicly suggesting that Zacharia reconsider the position. A White House official said she was being let go from the role. Her tenure had lasted only days.Susie Wiles: The powerful chief of staff facing questions about her own futureSusie Wiles has occupied one of the most influential positions in Trump's administration, serving as the gatekeeper to the president and a central figure in the operation of the West Wing. But reports of growing internal tensions have put her own position under the spotlight.Wiles, who helped lead Trump's successful 2024 presidential campaign, entered the second administration with a reputation for organisation and discipline. She became the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, a job that involves managing the president's schedule, coordinating senior aides and trying to ensure that the administration's priorities are carried out.Politico reported that Trump was considering replacing Wiles and was reaching out to people asking for names. But officially he dismissed the report calling it fake news and said Susie Wiles will be serving her role for a long time.One source of apparent friction between Trump and Susie Wiles was Trump's decision to approach Zacharia about becoming press secretary without consulting Wiles, according to people familiar with the appointment. The move was viewed internally as undermining the chief of staff and creating uncertainty about who was directing personnel decisions in the West Wing.Wiles has also faced pressure over the outside consulting work of longtime Trump allies Chris LaCivita and Tony Fabrizio Blair, who travelled to Republika Srpska in Bosnia for political consulting work. Trump publicly distanced himself from the two men and threatened to fire them if their work presented a conflict of interest.Wiles has also had a personal health challenge this year. In September, she announced that tests showed no remaining evidence of her breast cancer after treatment, saying she was grateful for the support she had received while continuing to work.Alina Habba: A multimillion-dollar dispute that has turned into a MAGA feudAlina Habba, the former personal attorney to Trump, has found herself at the centre of an extraordinary dispute involving a reported multimillion-dollar donation to the Kennedy Center and one of the president's former senior advisers. The controversy became public through an Axios report on October 14, which said Trump had directed White House counsel to examine allegations raised by Habba during a meeting at the White House. Habba reportedly told Trump that a donation her billionaire husband, Turkish businessman Turhan Mildon, intended for the Kennedy Center had not reached the institution.The amount at the centre of the dispute has varied in accounts of the episode. Axios reported that Habba initially cited a figure of $17 million, before the amount in question was narrowed to approximately $5.6 million. White House sources described it as nearly $6 million.The allegation involves Ric Grenell, the former president of the Kennedy Center and a longtime Trump ally. Habba alleged that Grenell had persuaded her husband to include a multimillion-dollar donation in a larger payment linked to a business deal involving a US company. She later discovered, according to the report, that the money did not appear in the Kennedy Center's records.Grenell has strongly denied the allegations. He called them absurd and said he had never asked for money to be sent elsewhere under the pretence that it was a Kennedy Center donation. The White House has sought documentation to support the claims, and an official cautioned that the allegations had not been established and could reflect a misunderstanding.Kristi Noem quietly moves to her third jobFormer DHS secretary Kristi Noem quietly moved to her third job in the Trump administration. After she was fired from her DHS role, she was made a special envoy which expired last month. Now, she will continue working on similar matters, CNN reported. “Kristi Noem’s envoy status expired last month and she is no longer in the role,” the official said. “She is now a Senior Advisor to Deputy Secretary Landau and continues to work on the Shield of the Americas portfolio.”Her ouster in March came after Noem told lawmakers that Trump approved of her agency’s lavish spending on an advertising campaign that prominently showcased her.Noem also filed for divorce from her husband Bryon Noem in September ending their 34 years of marriage.Kimberly Guilfoyle: The ambassador whose tenure ended amid a donor-payment controversyKimberly Guilfoyle's departure as US ambassador to Greece has become one of the most high-profile personnel controversies involving a Trump ally this month. A former Fox News host and California prosecutor, Guilfoyle was nominated for the diplomatic post after her engagement to Donald Trump Jr ended. She took up a role representing the United States in Athens, where she focused in part on energy cooperation and relations with Greece.But in October, reports about her dealings with a political donor placed her position under pressure. The Wall Street Journal reported that Guilfoyle had asked Trump donor Eric Deters to transfer $100,000 to cover her American Express bill before her confirmation hearing. According to the report, the messages suggested she would offer access to administration officials in return. Deters reportedly refused the request.The reporting also raised questions about travel and hospitality. The Wall Street Journal reported allegations involving private flights and luxury accommodation, while Guilfoyle's lawyers said she had followed State Department rules and denied that she had done anything wrong. Her legal team argued that the money she sought related to unpaid fees for speaking engagements that predated her ambassadorial nomination.Trump initially said he was considering whether to fire Guilfoyle. On October 13, the White House announced that she had been asked to resign. She announced her departure within hours, saying the allegations were false and that she intended to vigorously defend her reputation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
