articles.title: In 2022, a California owner agreed to a discounted $10 million sale of 402 acres despite approvals for 500+ homes; four years later, a land trust sued to stop permanent roads and utilities inside the preserve
articles.summary: A conservation group in California has filed a lawsuit to stop plans for permanent roads and utility lines across a newly created 402-acre nature preserve.
articles.body: A conservation group in California has filed a lawsuit to stop plans for permanent roads and utility lines across a newly created 402-acre nature preserve. The legal action comes four years after the land was saved from housing developers. Placer Land Trust filed the lawsuit to block infrastructure construction through Clover Valley, an area of oak woodland and wetlands in Rocklin, California. The group wants to protect the valley floor, which was bought at a reduced price of $10 million in 2022 after years of local opposition to housing projects. The dispute focuses on development rights that were attached to the property before it was protected. Before the land was purchased for conservation, the 402-acre site had full city approvals for more than 500 single-family homes and a major road crossing the valley.Decades of development pressureLocated in western Placer County, Clover Valley is one of the last remaining undeveloped oak woodland areas in the city of Rocklin. For more than 20 years, local residents and environmental groups have campaigned against plans to build housing subdivisions, roads and public infrastructure across the valley floor. The site has important natural and cultural features. Clover Valley Creek flows throughout the year and supports a 20-acre wetland that was partly formed by native beavers. The wetland provides a habitat for threatened bird species, including the California black rail and Swainson's hawk. Archaeological surveys have also found 34 prehistoric Native American sites across the property, including ancient bedrock mortars once used to prepare food. In 2022, the Christian institution Jessup University reached an agreement with the private landowner to buy the 402-acre valley floor for a reduced price of $10 million. This was despite the property having valid approvals for more than 500 homes.Funding and conservation easementTo complete the purchase and protect the land for the long term, Jessup University partnered with Placer Land Trust. Early efforts to obtain public conservation grants were delayed by California's state budget deficits. This led to a local fundraising campaign. According to public documents published by Placer Land Trust, the purchase was completed in early 2025 through a joint funding effort. Local government bodies, including Placer County, the Placer County Office of Education, the City of Rocklin and the City of Lincoln, provided financial support. More than $1.3 million was also raised from private donors. Under the agreement, Jessup University owns and manages the land. Placer Land Trust and Placer County jointly hold a permanent conservation easement, a legal agreement that restricts commercial and residential development on the property.Legal dispute over infrastructure rightsDespite the conservation easement being officially recorded, questions have returned over older rights to build infrastructure across the property. Four years after the initial sale agreement was reached, Placer Land Trust began legal proceedings to stop plans for permanent roads and utility lines through the preserve. According to public comments submitted to Placer County, local planning bodies and interest groups have debated whether earlier development approvals allow utility corridors and access roads to cross the valley floor to serve nearby properties. Placer Land Trust argues that allowing permanent utility installations or road construction would directly violate the conservation easement. The group says such work could damage the natural wetlands and historical sites that the agreement was created to protect. The lawsuit asks a court to confirm that the permanent conservation easement takes priority over earlier city development plans. The goal is to ensure that the 402-acre Clover Valley remains protected for nature, education and low-impact recreational activities.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2024, buyers paid $13.95 million for a Nantucket property and built a 13,500-sq-ft mansion with a private tunnel; two years later, it is asking $45 million and could set a Massachusetts record
articles.summary: On Nantucket, where old-world charm and serious real estate money have long shared the same narrow lanes, a brand-new mansion is making an unusually bold
articles.body: On Nantucket, where old-world charm and serious real estate money have long shared the same narrow lanes, a brand-new mansion is making an unusually bold entrance. Built after its owners acquired the property for $13.95 million in 2024, the sprawling Cliff Road residence has now arrived on the market for $45 million, a price that could rewrite Massachusetts’ residential sales record, states the latest report by Mansion Global.A new take on Nantucket classicAccording to Mansion Global, set on 0.62 acres in the highly coveted Cliff neighbourhood, the newly completed home stretches across 13,500 square feet and three levels. Its design leans firmly into Nantucket’s architectural vocabulary, with an unpainted cedar-shingle exterior, pitched roofs and dormer windows giving it the appearance of a grand New England summer house rather than a contemporary showpiece.Twin barn-style rooflines frame the main entrance, while matching double-gambrel volumes appear at both the front and rear of the residence. The scale is substantial, but the architecture remains rooted in the island’s traditional aesthetic. Nine bedrooms provide ample accommodation, while a roof walk offers elevated views across Nantucket Sound, one of the property’s most striking features, adds the latest online report.A house built around privacyThe property’s appeal extends well beyond the main residence. A pool and motor court add to its resort-like character, while a detached garage includes both a studio and a guest apartment. Perhaps the most unusual feature is hidden underground. The guest accommodation is connected to the main house by a private tunnel, adding a discreet layer of convenience and privacy to the estate, adds the report as well.From $13.95 million to $45 millionIf we go by the Mansion Global report, the sellers acquired the property through an LLC in 2024 from the estate of the late retail executive Roger Horchow. The original plan was reportedly to make the newly built home their own, but their plans changed after they developed a preference for another part of the island, where they had purchased an interim residence.The $45 million asking price would represent more than three times the property’s acquisition cost, although the figure reflects not just the land but the substantial construction and design investment that followed, explains the report.A potential Massachusetts recordMedia reports also claim that if the home sells close to its asking price, it could become the most expensive residential property ever sold in Massachusetts. The current benchmark stands at $43 million, set by the sale of a 31.5-acre estate on Martha’s Vineyard in September. Before that, a $42 million Nantucket waterfront purchase in 2023 had established another landmark for the state’s luxury property market.The new Cliff Road listing does not have a waterfront setting, but its location remains a major selling point. The Cliff is among Nantucket’s most sought-after neighbourhoods, combining proximity to the island’s attractions with the privacy and prestige that define its prime real estate. For a home that did not exist two years ago, its journey from a $13.95 million acquisition to a potential $45 million record is already a remarkable piece of Nantucket real estate history.Image Courtesy: Shane Riley/Great Point PropertiesReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: UP jail chief orders tighter surveillance, faster reforms across prisons
articles.summary: UP DG Prisons PC Meena orders faster prison reforms, stronger Jarvis CCTV monitoring, digitised staff records, and better facilities for women, children and disabled inmates.
articles.body: Lucknow: Uttar Pradesh director general of prisons and correctional services PC Meena on Friday directed jail authorities across the state to fast-track pending works, strengthen CCTV-based surveillance and improve facilities for vulnerable inmates, including women prisoners, children living in jails and persons with disabilities.Meena issued the instructions while chairing a statewide review meeting through video conference from the Prisons Headquarters in Lucknow.Officials were told to ensure that all pending assignments are completed within fixed timelines and that progress is monitored regularly to avoid slippages. As part of efforts to modernise prison administration, the DG reviewed the status of employee service records and staffing details on the Human Sampada portal.He instructed officers to complete data updation and ensure registration of all departmental posts on priority. Meena said digitisation of personnel records was necessary for more efficient and transparent administration, including smoother handling of postings, leave and service-related processes. Security and monitoring remained a central focus.Meena reviewed the connectivity and functioning of Jarvis CCTV cameras installed in prisons and their linkage with the central video wall at the Prisons Headquarters.He instructed jail authorities to ensure uninterrupted coverage and real-time monitoring of prison activities, stressing that technology-driven oversight was vital for maintaining order and preventing violations inside jails.The DG also examined proposals related to the transfer of inmates to Adarsh Karagars and sought updates on steps being taken to improve prison management and monitoring systems.On welfare measures, Meena reviewed district-level efforts for children residing with women inmates and directed officials to ensure regular monitoring and proper care arrangements.Accessibility for prisoners with disabilities was also reviewed, including the status of disability certificates, dedicated meeting facilities and infrastructure such as ramps. articles.title: Child sex abuse charges against Timothy Busfield tossed by New Mexico judge, citing prosecutor misconduct
articles.summary: A New Mexico judge has dismissed an indictment against “West Wing” and “Field of Dreams” actor Timothy Busfield that accused him of criminal sexual contact with a child, citing prosecutorial misconduct and errors that undermined the grand jury process.
articles.body: ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. — A New Mexico judge has dismissed an indictment against “West Wing” and “Field of Dreams” actor Timothy Busfield that accused him of criminal sexual contact with a child, citing prosecutorial misconduct and errors that undermined the grand jury process. State District Judge Joseph Montano granted a defense motion to toss the charges in a decision released Friday. Busfield has repeatedly denied the allegations, describing them as lies motivated by revenge. Prosecutors did not immediately say whether they would seek a new indictment. The case stems from when Busfield was directing the TV series “The Cleaning Lady” from 2022 to 2024. The parents of two twin boys who were let go from the show claimed that Busfield inappropriately touched the children on the set in Albuquerque. According to a criminal complaint filed in January, an investigator with the Albuquerque Police Department said a boy reported that Busfield touched him on his private areas over his clothing on one occasion when he was 7 years old and another time when he was 8. The boy’s twin brother told authorities he was also touched by Busfield, but he did not specify where and didn’t say anything because he didn’t want to get in trouble, the complaint said. Busfield turned himself in and was released from jail pending trial by a judge who found no pattern of criminal conduct or similar allegations involving children in Busfield’s past. The grand jury indictment followed just weeks later, reiterating allegations that Busfield “touched or applied force to the intimate parts” of one of the boys on several occasions. The indictment allowed the case to proceed without a preliminary hearing on evidence. Busfield’s attorneys noted that the children told police during initial interviews that Busfield didn’t touch them inappropriately and accused the boys’ parents of coaching their children to give incriminating statements after the boys lost lucrative roles on the show. In June, Busfield’s attorneys officially asked the court to throw out the indictment, alleging in a motion that prosecutors were “willfully blind to the lack of evidence” and “invented procedural hurdles” to keep grand jurors from hearing witness testimony. During a September hearing, Busfield’s attorney Amanda Fayerberg played audio recordings of grand jurors asking to hear from additional witnesses. Fayerberg said prosecutors wrongly informed jurors that subpoenas would be needed, even though those witnesses were “present, available and willing to testify.” “The state engaged in egregious prosecutorial misconduct,” Fayerberg said. Bernalillo County District Attorney Greer Staley countered that the defense hadn’t followed the correct process for submitting evidence to a grand jury and that Busfield himself improperly and “excessively” tried to steer grand jurors toward favorable witnesses and exhibits during his three-hour testimony. According to the transcripts of the proceedings submitted by Busfield’s attorneys, the actor also known for appearances in “Thirtysomething” told jurors that the case had turned his life upside down and affected his entire family. He testified that he had been “canceled,” meaning he lost work and was fired by his agency. Busfield also testified that he had nothing to hide and when asked about the allegations that he had caressed the children, he answered: “I’m saying that is absolutely one gazillion percent untrue. Never ever.” Prosecutors had said each count in the indictment carried a possible penalty of six years in prison that could be enhanced.
